Virtual circuits instead of dedicated circuits

Frame Relay is a layer 2 protocol derived from HDLC and connection-oriented. It provides neither quality of service nor error recovery, and it is implemented over speeds from n × 64 kb up to 34 Mbps.

Traditionally, sites were joined through the telephone network, which sets up dedicated circuits: it reserves a 64 kb slot, dedicated exclusively to that communication.

On a packet network you contract an access and a virtual circuit: a logical configuration in the nodes stating that one subscriber communicates with another. No resources are reserved: the link is shared among everyone, which is why it is cheaper.
Dedicated circuit = physical resource for exclusive use. Virtual circuit = logical configuration over a shared link.

With links to the headquarters you build a star: all branch offices access its services, but to connect two branch offices you must go through headquarters.

A mesh with dedicated circuits forces you to contract an enormous number of circuits (in red) that are barely used: expensive and inefficient.

With Frame Relay each site contracts one access to the network and the provider connects it to the others through virtual circuits. They are almost always permanent (PVC); switched ones, similar to a phone call for data, are less popular.
Adding a site to the mesh means contracting an access and requesting virtual circuits, not laying dedicated circuits.
DLCI: which circuit each frame belongs to

Over a single access, several logical communications to different destinations travel multiplexed. Each one is identified with a DLCI (data link connection identifier), an idea similar to the 802.1Q VLAN tag.

Each node has a table: what comes in through a port with a DLCI goes out through another port with another DLCI. In the example, what arrives on Port 0 with DLCI 16 leaves on Port 2 with DLCI 30.

The PVC ends up established as the concatenation of those DLCIs, node by node. It is a static configuration loaded by the provider: for each new service it assigns a DLCI and fills in the tables.
The DLCI does not stay the same end to end: each node changes it according to its table.

The format is defined by LAPF, the core version of Frame Relay: it is the user plane, and covers only some of the data link layer functions. Separately there is a control plane, with a protocol for connecting two endpoints with switched virtual circuits.

  • Flag: the same as HDLC, with zero insertion.
  • Address: 2 bytes minimum, extendable to 3 or 4. Unlike HDLC, there is no control field.
  • Data: variable length, up to 4096 bytes (generally 1600).
  • FCS: the same as HDLC, a CRC-16.

DLCI: 6 + 4 = 10 bits, i.e., 2¹⁰ possible circuits (more if the address takes 3 or 4 bytes). EA (Extended Address): 0 if the field continues, 1 in the last byte. C/R: command / response. FECN and BECN: congestion notifications. DE: when 1, the frame is discard-eligible.
CIR and EIR: committed and excess

Data traffic is asymmetric: an HTTP GET is a small request and the response can carry megabytes. A fixed-capacity circuit does not fit: the ideal is to have a lot of capacity, but only when it is needed.

Frame Relay distinguishes two rates within the access:

  • CIR (committed information rate): what the provider guarantees to carry.
  • EIR (excess information rate): what is consumed above the CIR. It is not guaranteed: it is transmitted if there is room in the network.

For example, a 2 Mb access with a 256 kb CIR. In the next steps we use a 128 kb access with a 64 kb CIR and 64 kb of EIR.
If the network is congested, the provider guarantees that it will at least let the CIR through.
Bits transmitted during a Tc of 1 second

Tc: interval during which the transmission rate is measured.
Bc: maximum number of bits the network guarantees to deliver during Tc.
Be: maximum number of bits above the CIR that the network will try to deliver during Tc.

CIR = Bc / Tc  ·  EIR = Be / Tc
With Tc = 1 s and Bc = 64 kb, the CIR is 64 kb per second.
Traffic management I: below the CIR

The node we are connected to performs traffic control: it checks that the commitment is met using a counter that restarts at every Tc.

A frame of X bits comes in and the counter reads X. Another of Y comes in: X + Y. A third of Z comes in: X + Y + Z.

All three arrived within the same second and add up to less than 64 kb: they are below the CIR, inside the committed area.

The node lets them through with the DE = 0 bit. When DE is 1, the frame is discard-eligible.
As long as traffic stays below the CIR, all frames travel as committed.
Three frames in a Tc of 1 second
Example values: 20 + 18 + 22 = 60 kb, less than the 64 kb committed.
Traffic management II: in the excess zone

Now, in the same interval, four frames are transmitted whose sum exceeds the committed limit.

The first three remain below the CIR: they pass with DE = 0.

The fourth crosses the threshold and enters the EIR zone: it was transmitted in excess, and the node sets DE = 1 on it.

The network carries all the traffic as long as it has capacity. But if any node experiences congestion, it drops the frames with DE = 1 first, because they are above what was committed.
DE = 1 is not a drop: it is the mark of what can be dropped first if needed.
Four frames in a Tc of 1 second
With frame 4 the counter reaches 90 kb: it passes the 64 kb of CIR, but not the 128 kb of CIR + EIR.
Traffic management III: beyond CIR + EIR

Third case: traffic is sent above the CIR and the EIR. This can happen, for example, when what you want to send to the server exceeds the CIR + EIR.

Frames that exceed CIR + EIR are dropped at ingress: they never even enter the network.

Thus, within one interval there are frames that travel as committed (DE = 0), others that are marked (DE = 1), and others that are simply dropped.

Frame Relay does not handle the dropped frames: the upper layers do, and they will retransmit.
Three regions: DE = 0 up to Bc, DE = 1 up to Bc + Be, and rejection above.
Four larger frames in a Tc of 1 second
Frame 4 would bring the counter to 145 kb: it exceeds the 128 kb of CIR + EIR.

Frame Relay does no flow control: if one station transmits above the other's capacity, it overloads it.

It does no congestion control either: it only notifies the endpoints, using two bits of the frame.

  • FECN (Forward Explicit Congestion Notification): notifies forward. Whoever receives it knows that a node along the path is experiencing congestion.
  • BECN (Backward Explicit Congestion Notification): notifies backward. It tells whoever is injecting a lot of traffic to reduce its transmission rate, because it is one of those involved.
The network warns; reacting is up to the endpoints.
FECN follows the direction of transmission; BECN goes back toward the source of the traffic.

• Layer 2, derived from HDLC and connection-oriented; no QoS, error recovery, or flow control.
  • Virtual circuits (generally PVC) over shared links: the mesh becomes viable.
  • The DLCI identifies each circuit; nodes switch it using a port / DLCI table.
  • CIR guaranteed (DE = 0), EIR in excess (DE = 1), and drop above CIR + EIR.
  • FECN / BECN only notify congestion.
